title: What an operating system is
subtitle: One program that manages every other: it shares the hardware, hides its ugliness, and draws the line between trusted and untrusted code.

sections.title: Two jobs in one
sections.body:
An operating system does two things. It is an extended machine: it hides the raw hardware behind clean abstractions — files instead of disk sectors, processes instead of a shared CPU, sockets instead of network cards. And it is a resource manager: it decides who gets the CPU, memory and devices, and stops programs from trampling each other.

The kernel is the part that always runs in privileged mode. Around it sit the shell (the command interpreter), utilities and applications, which run in user mode and reach the kernel only through system calls.

questions.prompt: Why can a user program not simply call a kernel function directly?

choices.text: Because kernel functions are written in a different language.
Because it would be too slow.
User code runs unprivileged; a system call is the controlled doorway that switches the CPU into kernel mode.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Language is irrelevant. The barrier is hardware-enforced privilege, not syntax.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Speed is not the reason — protection is.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The trap instruction changes the privilege level and jumps to a fixed, checked entry point. Without it any program could read another’s memory or rewrite the disk.

figures.caption: Figure 1.1.1 — layers of a system
figures.note: A request travels down through the system-call boundary; the answer comes back up.
figures.script:
diagram("direction: down
[Applications] as app #blue
[Shell and utilities] as sh #blue
[System-call interface] as sc #amber
[Kernel: scheduler, memory, file system, drivers] as k #violet
[Hardware: CPU, RAM, disk, network] as hw #grey
app -> sc : open(), read(), fork()
sh -> sc
sc -> k
k -> hw
@0 app -> sc : read()
@1.2 sc -> k : trap
@2.4 k -> hw : disk I/O
loop 4");

sections.title: Kinds of kernel
sections.body: A monolithic kernel (classic Unix, Linux) runs everything — scheduler, file systems, drivers — in one address space: fast, but a buggy driver can crash the machine. A microkernel keeps only the essentials (scheduling, IPC, basic memory) in the kernel and runs the rest as user-mode servers: safer and easier to extend, but every service call costs a message. Layered kernels stack strict layers; hybrid kernels (Windows NT, macOS) mix the two; exokernels expose raw hardware and leave abstraction to libraries.

questions.prompt: What is the main price of a microkernel?

choices.text: It cannot run on modern hardware.
More message passing between user-mode servers, so each service call is slower.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Microkernels (QNX, seL4, Mach-based systems) run well on modern hardware.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Quite the opposite: protection between services is its selling point.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Isolation is bought with context switches and copies: a file read becomes a message to the file server and a reply.

figures.caption: Figure 1.2.1 — two kernel designs
figures.note: Where the boundary sits decides speed versus isolation.
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
group "Monolithic" { m1, m2 }
group "Microkernel" { u1, u2, mk }
[Everything in one kernel] as m1 #violet
[Hardware] as m2 #grey
[File server] as u1 #blue
[Driver] as u2 #blue
[Tiny kernel: IPC, scheduling, memory] as mk #violet
m1 -> m2
u1 -> mk : message
u2 -> mk : message");

sections.title: From power button to login
sections.body: At power-on the CPU runs firmware from a fixed address. Legacy BIOS loads the first 512-byte sector — the MBR — which chain-loads a bootloader; modern UEFI reads a bootloader from an EFI system partition on a GPT disk directly, and can verify its signature (secure boot). The bootloader loads the kernel into memory and jumps to it; the kernel initialises devices, mounts the root file system and starts the first user process (init/systemd), which starts everything else.

worked.why: Firmware finds the boot device and reads sector 0 (512 bytes).
The 446-byte boot code plus the 64-byte partition table plus the 2-byte signature fill the sector: 446 + 64 + 2 = 512.

questions.prompt: Why is the MBR bootloader so small?

choices.text: It must fit in one 512-byte sector the firmware can read before any file system exists.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: One sector is nothing on a modern disk; the limit comes from what firmware loads, not from capacity.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The firmware knows nothing about files; it can only read sector 0. That tiny code loads a bigger loader that does understand file systems.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Kernels are megabytes; the MBR code only starts the chain.

figures.caption: Figure 1.3.1 — the boot chain
figures.note: Each stage is small and loads the next, bigger one.

sections.title: A zoo of operating systems
sections.body: Mainframe and server systems maximise throughput and uptime; personal systems favour responsiveness; smartphone and embedded systems live with tight power and memory; real-time systems guarantee that a task finishes by its deadline (hard) or usually does (soft). The same ideas — processes, memory, files — appear in all of them with different priorities.

questions.prompt: What defines a hard real-time system?

choices.text: Missing a deadline is a failure, not merely a slowdown.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Speed helps, but the requirement is a guaranteed bound, not raw speed.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Real-time systems multitask routinely; they schedule to meet deadlines.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Anti-lock brakes or a pacemaker must respond within a bound; predictability matters more than average speed.

figures.caption: Figure 1.4.1 — system types
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
[Batch / mainframe] as a #grey
[Server] as b #blue
[Desktop] as c #mint
[Mobile / embedded] as d #amber
[Real-time] as e #rose
a -> b : interactive, networked
b -> c : GUI, single user
c -> d : power, size limits
d -> e : deadlines");

problems.prompt: Name three system calls and what each asks the kernel to do.
problems.answer: open() — the file system finds a file and returns a handle; fork() — the process manager duplicates the calling process; read() — a driver fetches bytes from a file or device into the caller’s buffer.

problems.prompt: Compare a monolithic kernel and a microkernel in one sentence each.
problems.answer: Monolithic: all services in one privileged address space — fast, less isolated. Microkernel: minimal privileged core plus user-mode services — isolated, slower because of message passing.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• OS = extended machine + resource manager.
  • User mode ↔ kernel mode only through system calls.
  • Kernel designs trade speed against isolation.
  • Boot is a chain of ever-larger loaders.
